title: Effects of Sulfate Limitation on a 1,2,3‐Trichloropropane‐Dechlorinating Consortium: Isotopic Evidence and Community Succession
content:
Long-term sulfate limitation induces taxonomic-functional decoupling in a TCP-dechlorinating consortium. Despite a community shift from sulfate-reducers to fermentative/syntrophic guilds, metabolic rewiring—enriching Geobacter as electron hubs—sustains robust dechlorination kinetics and conserved isotope fractionation, ensuring functional resilience.


ABSTRACT

1,2,3-Trichloropropane (TCP) is a persistent groundwater contaminant, and its efficient detoxification relies heavily on microbial reductive dechlorination. The in situ application of microbial bioremediation systems is often challenged by dynamic fluctuations in groundwater geochemical conditions, particularly the spatiotemporal heterogeneity of electron acceptors. How functional microbial consortia respond to such environmental perturbations to sustain core degradation functions represents a critical ecological question determining the success of in situ remediation. To investigate this adaptive mechanism, this study established a long-term (three-year, > 100 generations) parallel acclimation experiment. Using the transition from electron-acceptor-replete (sulfate-rich) to electron-acceptor-limited conditions as a representative environmental perturbation scenario, we systematically evaluated the response strategies of the consortium by integrating degradation kinetics, compound-specific isotope analysis (CSIA), and metagenomics. Results indicated that despite significant shifts in electron acceptor availability, the macroscopic degradation kinetics and carbon isotope fractionation characteristics (ε C) remained highly consistent. Conversely, the microbial community exhibited apparent taxonomic-functional decoupling, undergoing a structural succession from a sulfur-metabolism-driven assemblage to a fermentation- and syntrophy-driven consortium. Metagenomic analysis suggests that the community adapted via metabolic network rewiring. Specifically, this involved the selective enrichment of taxa capable of efficient electron transfer (e.g., Geobacter) and reliance on auxiliary taxa (e.g., Parabacteroides) for the stable supply of essential cofactors (vitamin B12), thereby supporting the syntrophic dechlorination pathway under resource limitation. Ultimately, this study illustrates that functional consortia can sustain core metabolic processes under environmental stress through modular network restructuring. These findings validate the bioremediation potential of the consortium under complex hydrochemical conditions and provide a robust ecological basis for developing environmentally adaptive in situ remediation strategies.
